1.pericope_label: And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him. Then answered Peter, and said unto Jesus, Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias. While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him. And when the disciples heard it, they fell on their face, and were sore afraid. And Jesus came and touched them, and said, Arise, and be not afraid. And when they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no man, save Jesus only.

schools.summary: Robertson allows the plain sixth day but thinks a week likelier, since Luke says about eight, and identifies the verb as the one behind the metamorphoses of the poets, touching the form and not the outward fashion; he also marks the difference from the baptism, where the same words were addressed to Jesus and here are spoken to the disciples about him. Ellicott explains Luke's looser phrase by the reckoning that called some six-and-thirty hours three days, notes that the three keep the place they held at the raising of the ruler's daughter, thinks the recognition of the two visitants intuitive, and adds that it was not good for frail men to tarry in that Presence. Barnes takes the word for a change of appearance and not of substance, explains the choice of Moses as the giver of the law whose types were being fulfilled, and reads the cloud as diffused over the disciples rather than darkening them. Lightfoot makes the whole scene a thing of the night.

Calvin asks whether Moses and Elijah were really present or only shown in vision, as the prophets often saw absent things, and judges it more probable that they were actually brought there; he finds in Peter's offer a fear that the sight would vanish when the visitors left, and does not wonder that Peter was so captivated. On the closing words he says the Law and the Prophets had a temporary glory so that Christ alone might remain in view, and that a man who would use Moses rightly must not stop with him but be led by his hand to Christ. Gill guards the change from being taken for more than it was, neither the substance of the body nor its shape altered, only a more glorious form received.

Clarke and Wesley agree in making the transfiguration a disclosure rather than an alteration, the fullness of the Godhead that dwelt bodily in Christ shining out through the human nature, the indwelling Deity darting its rays through the veil of the flesh, so that he no longer bore the form of a servant. Clarke presses the bodies of the visitants, Elijah coming in the body he was translated in and Moses probably raised as a pledge of the resurrection. Wesley calls Peter's words rapturous surprise and notices the arithmetic, three tents and not six, because the apostles meant to stay with their Master; on the voice from the cloud he reduces the command to its point, that they hear him as superior even to Moses and the prophets.
Henry reads the scene as an earnest of the kingdom Christ had just spoken of, a pledge given to the three rather than a wonder standing on its own account.

Chrysostom asks why Jesus waited six days and gives two reasons, that the other disciples might not be touched with jealousy and that those going up might be kindled with more desire in the interval. On the cloud he contrasts Sinai, where the darkness was meant to terrify, with this brightness, whose purpose was to teach, and observes that neither Moses nor Elijah speaks but the Father.
Origen takes the six days mystically: in six days the whole visible world was made, so a man who rises above the things of this world may climb the mountain and see the glory of the Word.
Leo calls the lesson a great mystery, better understood if we attend to what is narrated just before it.

9.pericope_label: And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, saying, Tell the vision to no man, until the Son of man be risen again from the dead. And his disciples asked him, saying, Why then say the scribes that Elias must first come? And Jesus answered and said unto them, Elias truly shall first come, and restore all things. But I say unto you, That Elias is come already, and they knew him not, but have done unto him whatsoever they listed. Likewise shall also the Son of man suffer of them. Then the disciples understood that he spake unto them of John the Baptist.

schools.summary: Barnes takes the vision as meant to confirm the three that he was the Messiah, so that while he remained with them there was no need to report it, and holds the scribes' doctrine of Elijah's coming true, since Jesus does not deny it but adds that Elijah has come. Ellicott points out that the prohibition covered the other apostles too, who would have distrusted or perverted the report, thinks the question came from the three alone, brooding over the appearance and still more the disappearance of Elijah, and finds the words about restoring deliberately enigmatic, admitting two very different interpretations. Robertson puts the difficulty exactly, that they had just seen Elijah but the Messiah had come before him and the scribes had Malachi on their side, and distinguishes John as the fulfilment of the promise from the Elijah in person that John denied being. Lightfoot supplies what the rabbis expected of the restorer, the purifying of doubtful births and the bringing back of the pot of manna, the vial of holy oil and the vial of water.

Calvin says plainly that the disciples themselves would not have believed the vision without the more striking proof of the resurrection, traces their confusion further back, since no sooner is the resurrection mentioned than they imagine the reign of Christ already begun, and explains the root of the scribes' error, that John was to resemble Elijah in restoring a fallen Church and Malachi had given him that name, which they interpreted rashly. Gill notes that it was the account of the ill usage which made the identification plain.

Wesley gives both halves of the danger in the silence imposed, that the rest would be grieved at not being admitted and outsiders either enraged or, when the sufferings came, incredulous; he hears in the disciples' question an objection to that silence, and states the identification in the Baptist's own words, that he was not Elijah the Tishbite come again but the man of whom the prophecy spoke under that name. Clarke adds a political reason for the silence, that a matter certain to irritate the Jewish rulers was better kept quiet, and notes that some manuscripts read simply the disciples, meaning those who had been on the mount.

Chrysostom observes that the disciples learned the coming of Elijah not from the Scriptures but from the scribes, whose teaching had become current among the ignorant multitude, as their teaching about Christ had.

Origen uses the verse to refuse transmigration outright: that Elijah is already come is not to be understood of the soul of Elijah, lest we fall into metempsychosis, which is foreign to the truth of the Church's doctrine, but of one who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, as the angel foretold.
Augustine takes the restoring of all things forward instead, of those whom the persecution of Antichrist shall have overthrown, as Christ himself restores by his death.

debates.question: What does the restoring of all things mean?

Deliberately enigmatic, admitting two very different interpretations, one of them an Elijah still to come

14.pericope_label: And when they were come to the multitude, there came to him a certain man, kneeling down to him, and saying, Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water. And I brought him to thy disciples, and they could not cure him. Then Jesus answered and said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him hither to me. And Jesus rebuked the devil; and he departed out of him: and the child was cured from that very hour. Then came the disciples to Jesus apart, and said, Why could not we cast him out? And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you. Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.

schools.summary: Robertson glosses the boy's disorder as moonstruck, the symptoms of epilepsy being supposed to worsen with the changes of the moon, and calls little faith a good rendering, theirs being less than a grain of mustard seed. Barnes and Robertson both explain the word rendered perverse as twisted or turned out of its proper direction, and Barnes takes the seed for the smallest of seeds, so that the feeblest genuine faith would serve. Ellicott notes from Luke that the descent was on the next day, divides the rebuke between scribes and disciples as both wanting the faith that utters itself in prayer, observes that the question about the failure came from those left below, and prefers the harder reading of unbelief, finding the variant a specimen of the tendency to tone down the severity of our Lord's words. Lightfoot says the edge of the rebuke is levelled especially at the scribes, though the disciples are not untouched.

Calvin agrees that though the words appear addressed to the father they are meant for the scribes, the reproof not being for the ignorant and weak; he says the disciples wondered at a power taken away which they had lost by their own fault, and reads the last verse of this kind of devils, adding that Christ was reproving negligence by showing that no ordinary faith was required. Gill places the conversation in a house, apart from the crowd, and takes the same reading of the kind meant.

Wesley reconciles the medical and the theological accounts of the disorder, that the word is used with propriety though the case was preternatural, an evil spirit taking advantage of the moon's influence on brain and nerves; he calls the last verse a testimony to the efficacy of fasting added to fervent prayer, noting that other kinds the apostles had cast out without it. Clarke insists the lunacy was still occasioned by a demon, puts the disciples' failure sharply, that they were confounded at their want of success but not at their want of faith which caused it, and reports but rejects the reading that refers the phrase to the faith which does not exert itself but by prayer and fasting.
Henry sets the scene as a melancholy case brought to Christ the moment he came down from the glory above.

Chrysostom draws out what the father's words imply about providence, that a demon who threw the boy into fire and water would have killed him outright had God not restrained him, and says the disciples feared they had forfeited the power over unclean spirits once given them.

Origen makes the descent a rebuke of the request just refused, since Peter had preferred his own benefit in wishing to stay, but charity seeks not her own; he makes the perversity of the generation a thing contrary to nature that enters stealthily and distorts, and turns the mustard seed round, that faith is like it because it is looked on with contempt and shows as something poor and mean, yet falling on a good heart becomes a great tree.

Augustine reads the fire and water morally, the fire of anger that aims upward and the water of fleshly lust, and takes the mountain to be removed as earthly pride, against which disciples working miracles are warned. Gregory presses the mustard seed further, that it gives out its qualities only when bruised, so that persecution rouses in a holy man what had seemed weak into the heat of virtue.

22.pericope_label: And while they abode in Galilee, Jesus said unto them, The Son of man shall be betrayed into the hands of men: And they shall kill him, and the third day he shall be raised again. And they were exceeding sorry.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers as they went to and fro to while they abode in Galilee, the journeying being unconnected with the work of the ministry, notes Mark's statement that he would not that any man should know of their presence and Luke's charge that these sayings sink down into your ears, and finds that the repetition gave the announcement new force rather than the air of a passing foreboding; on the closing verse he reads their sorrow as vague and dim, since Mark and Luke say they understood not and were afraid to ask. Barnes takes the betrayal in the strict sense of delivering up in a treacherous manner, as Judas did who used the confidence reposed in him, and offers three reasons for the disciples' failure to understand, their attachment to him, their unwillingness to believe it, and their expectation of a distinguished Prince who would restore the kingdom to Israel. Robertson reads the exceeding sorrow the other way, as a sign that they at last understood he was talking about his death and resurrection.

Calvin explains why the warning had to be repeated, that the nearer the death approached the more often Christ spoke of it lest the spectacle give a violent shock to their faith, and finds them alarmed as if nothing of it had ever reached their ears, so great is the influence of preconceived opinion, which brings darkness over the mind in the midst of the clearest light; they had imagined a kingdom prosperous and delightful and never thought it possible that the rulers of the Church would oppose him. Gill notes that this is the third time the warning is given, as they moved on toward Judea and the passover, so that the disciples might be prepared for the death and not terrified by it.

Clarke follows Grotius and Wakefield in holding that the verb should be rendered delivered up rather than betrayed, and the agency referred to God rather than to Judas, with the prayer of Acts 4:27-28 for warrant.

Henry dwells on the phrase into the hands of men, men to whom he was allied by nature and from whom he might have expected pity, men he had undertaken to save and from whom he might have expected gratitude, and these are his persecutors and murderers; nothing less than his blood would satisfy their rage, and nothing less would answer his own undertaking, since without blood there is no remission. He notes that whenever Christ spoke of his death he gave a hint of the resurrection, the joy set before him for which he endured the cross.
Chrysostom makes a narrower version of the same point about the three days, that this is no long time to speak of continuing in death.

Origen denies that the Lord is simply repeating himself, since what is new is that he must be delivered into the hands of men, and holds both agencies at once, that the Son was delivered up by the Father according to Romans 8:32 while different powers gave him into the hands of men.

Both at once, the Father according to Romans 8:32 and different powers into the hands of men

24.pericope_label: And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received tribute money came to Peter, and said, Doth not your master pay tribute? He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers? Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free. Notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money: that take, and give unto them for me and thee.

schools.summary: Barnes identifies the didrachma as the temple rate of Exodus 30 rather than a Roman tax, takes the argument plainly, that kings do not tax their own sons and the Son of God for whom the money is gathered cannot lawfully be required to pay it, and prefers foreknowledge to creation in the matter of the coin. Ellicott thinks the collectors' question implies they half suspected the Prophet of Nazareth would disclaim payment, argues that the exemption reaches wider than the single case, since on the narrow reading the Israelites who paid would be aliens rather than sons, and makes the saying a judgment against the Pharisees, who had lately carried in the Sanhedrin the point that the temple rate be compulsory; on the coin he alone hesitates, since there is no record that the miracle was wrought and the wonder stands alone in its kind. Robertson notes that the tax fell due in the month Adar and was nearly six months overdue, calls the sons logically free but practically not, and treats the stater as a miracle of foreknowledge, rejecting the older rationalist readings as a nervous anxiety to relieve the Gospel of the miraculous. Lightfoot supports the identification from Josephus and from the Talmudists, who speak of those that collect the shekels where Matthew has those that receive the didrachma.

Calvin dissents from the common identification, taking the didrachma for the sacred tax that the kings of Asia and then the Romans appropriated, so that the Jews paid to profane tyrants what they had formerly paid to God alone; on the coin he says the point was to prove a dominion wider than any earthly king's, the sea itself paying him tribute. Gill notes that Christ did not stay away from Capernaum to avoid the demand, and applies the reason given for payment to the duty of giving no offence to Jew or Gentile or the church of God, even at our own disadvantage.

Clarke insists the tax was not paid to the Roman government but for the support of the temple, extends the exemption to the disciples as ministering priests were exempt, and lays out the alternatives for the coin, that it was already in the fish, that the fish was impelled to fetch it, or that it was created for the purpose, any of which shows wisdom or power. Wesley agrees that the payment was voluntary, a thing which custom rather than any law had established.

Henry notes that Christ came to Capernaum rather than staying away, Peter keeping the house there and being presumed to know his Master's mind; he draws the rule that prudence and humility teach us to recede from our right rather than give offence by insisting on it, though we must never decline a duty for that reason, and observes that the coin was exactly enough for two and no more, Christ making the fish his cash keeper and teaching us not to covet superfluities.
Chrysostom explains why the collectors came to Peter from the origin of the tax in the redemption of the firstborn, so that they came to the firstborn son through the first among the disciples.
Origen turns the terms of the question over: the sons of the kings of the earth are not the free ones, since whoever sins is the servant of sin, and the free are those who abide in the word.

Augustine puts the argument shortest, that if children are free in every kingdom, much more are they free who are children of that kingdom under which all the kingdoms of the earth lie. Gregory sets the limit of the principle of avoiding offence: we must cast about how to avoid scandalising our neighbours as far as we may without sin, but if offence is taken from truth, it is better that offence should come than that truth be forsaken.

positions.position: The temple rate of Exodus 30, not a payment to the Roman government
The sacred tax once paid to God, appropriated by the kings of Asia and then the Romans, so that it went to profane tyrants
